To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the present boundary-layer prediction scheme is accurate for small low-speed wind tunnel contractions, and that the accuracy of the scheme is not seriously degraded by the use of a three-dimensional method to calculate the wall pressure distribution.

(i) the three-dimensional potential-flow theory is a useful tool for the calculation of the wall pressure distributions in small, low speed contractions and that (ii) the assumption of a two-dimensional, laminar boundary layer is a reasonable approximation for the calculation of boundary-layer growth in small, low- speed contraction sections.

(1) the wall velocity profiles for small low-speed contraction sections are predicted accurately by a three-dimensional potential flow method, (2) the boundary layers on the walls of small low-speed contraction are predicted accurately by the boundary-layer integral equations of the Falkner-Skan type, and (3) the measured boundary layer thicknesses at the contraction exits are within 10% of the predicted values.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the prediction of boundary layer development for the family of small, low speed contractions.
the development of an accurate and efficient method for the prediction of the boundary-layer development in a wind-tunnel contraction section.

the development of a method of prediction of boundary-layer behavior in low-speed wind tunnel contractions, and with the verification of this method by means of experiments in the 6-inch low-speed wind tunnel at N.A.C.A.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the boundary-layer prediction method described in this report is capable of predicting the wall velocity distributions and boundary-layer momentum thicknesses to within about 15 percent of the measured values.
for the family of contrations treated the method is accurate to within 10 percent for the prediction of the boundary layer momentum thickness at the exit of small, low-speed contraction sections.
the present method of predicting the boundary layer behavior in small low-speed wind tunnel contractions is adequate for design purposes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the present family of contractions, the boundary layer development is well predicted by the present scheme.
the agreement between predicted and measured boundary-layer development is quite satisfactory, and that the method of predicting the wall pressure distributions is adequate.

, with the exception of a small region near the contraction throat, the boundary layer is laminar and that the potential-flow method of predicting wall velocity distribution, when combined with boundary-layer theory, yields a very good prediction of boundary-layer growth.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the boundary layer development is very sensitive to the contraction wall geometry, and that the boundary layer thickness at the exit of a small contraction is not necessarily a reliable indicator of the quality of the flow.

the potential-flow method used to calculate wall pressure distributions is capable of predicting boundary-layer development in low-speed contractions with an accuracy comparable to that of the boundary-layer integral equations.
the boundary layers on contraction sidewalls are very sensitive to the details of the sidewall geometry.
